tools.title: After an extraordinary wave, what comes next?
tools.summary_raw: The “smart” conventional wisdom is: midterms don’t predict future elections. I’m not sure about that for a profoundly unpopular lame duck.
tools.content_text: George W. Bush, deep into his lame-duck term, after addressing the nation on the Iraq War in Sept. 2007. Getty Images. We’d like to extend another word of thanks for following FLIPR , our midterm election coverage , and our liveblog last night . We’re really pleased with how everything went, and I can’t express how much more fulfilling it is to run our own business than to work for a big, careless corporation . I do need to catch up on rest after we published seven stories, plus the liveblog, within a three-day window. That’s not typical for us; we aim for something more like three newsletters per week, plus regularly updating a host of models and statistical tools . Nor are those all politics posts; we also regularly cover sports , AI and sometimes some “ wild card ” topics. (To control what types of emails appear in your inbox, see here .) I’m also aware that one can go overboard on post-election recriminations: I think we probably did that in 2024, for instance. On our agenda for the year ahead: rebuilding RAPTOR (our NBA model) and possibly extending PELE, our soccer model, to European club football; beginning our coverage of the 2028 presidential election (sorry, not sorry), probably including some polling tools; expanding our coverage of AI; and a site redesign. We also may be doing some hiring. Subscribe now Still, last night’s results deserve deeper consideration than most elections. As measured by the change in the House popular vote, they featured the second-biggest midterm swing since World War II, which should be around 15 points toward Democrats once all votes are counted. Democrats will gain 7 to 9 Senate seats — Alaska and Mississippi are pending — along with flipping around 45 House seats and, once all votes are counted in Kansas, probably 6 governorships. Unlike some recent Democratic maps that were concentrated in smaller coastal states, these occurred broadly in basically every corner of the country. (Well, except Florida, as usual .) Once new terms begin, Democrats will control the governorships in states totaling around three-quarters of the U.S. population; in the Electoral College, this would translate to a 392-146 landslide. 1 There were plenty of signature wins too. Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932. Not only did James Talarico win by double digits in Texas; Gina Hinojosa flipped the governorship there. Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation’s first Black female governor. They won a Senate seat in South Carolina, and if prediction markets are right , they’ll flip Mississippi too. The repudiation that Democrats have been waiting 10 years for against Donald Trump finally came, and bigly. Friend-of-the-newsletter Sean Trende has written that this was a “ 100-year flood ”, the usual nomenclature of waves and tsunamis not quite sufficing. […]

market.title: Nigeria Health Watch builds AI-readiness with an internal wiki
market.summary_raw: The non-profit organisation is developing an AI-driven solution for documenting and retaining internal resources, with strong potential to save its employees’ time and give them better access to institutional knowledge.
market.content_text: About the organisation : Nigeria Health Watch is a communication and advocacy non-profit focused on improving health outcomes in Nigeria. Originally launched as a two-person blog in 2007, it has since expanded into a broader organisation that today is involved in solutions-driven journalism, community health monitoring, advocacy and research. Its team of permanent and freelance staff and volunteers comprises more than 60 people. Building the ‘brain of the organisation’ To some degree, every organisation struggles with institutional knowledge. As years go by and staff members come and go, it’s seemingly unavoidable that documents, multimedia files and other resources become scattered and effectively lost across online platforms, servers and local hard drives. This was the problem that Nigeria Health Watch tackled during their participation in NextGen AI Leaders , a WAN-IFRA programme in partnership with the Google News Initiative. The programme is designed to help young media leaders reach the next stage in their careers through responsible AI deployment and strategic leadership. During the programme, Chibuike Alagboso , Director of Media Programmes at Nigeria Health Watch, began the process of building an internal wiki, a “brain of the organisation,” in order to better preserve organisational memory. According to Alagboso, there was a strong feeling within the organisation that access to important resources tends to disappear, especially after employees leave: “You might as well not have those materials, because they are scattered all over the place and you can’t access them. You might not even know they exist.” Even when a specific file is needed for a project – a concept note, or a photograph – “we often find ourselves in situations where we have to spend a lot of time looking for it,” he said. Start with a vibe-coded prototype Today, Nigeria Health Watch is involved in a wide range of activities, but the organisation’s roots go back to a blog that was started by two friends interested in covering health care in the country. That foundation is still strong, Alagboso said: “We still write, we still produce content, we’re very active on social media.” The organisation’s regular output includes thought-leadership and opinion pieces, and it has a particular focus on solutions journalism. Before joining the NextGen AI Leaders programme, Nigeria Health Watch had explored various types of AI use, from content generation and social media amplification to transcription, summarisation and analysis of large troves of documents. As Alagboso began to develop an internal wiki to better capture organisational knowledge and resources – their most ambitious AI-driven initiative to date – his first step was to build a prototype that he could share with the IT team. market.title: WAN-IFRA condemns arrest of Japanese journalist
market.summary_raw: The Hokkaido Shimbun correspondent was seized while preparing his departure from Sakhalin Island, accused of gathering information on Russia's defences. The global press body says security laws must not be used to punish public-interest reporting or turn reporters into bargaining pawns.
market.content_text: WAN-IFRA, the World Association of News Publishers, condemns the criminalisation of journalism in Russia and has called on Russian authorities to immediately release Japanese journalist, Yuki Imai, detained on allegations of espionage. Imai, an accredited Japanese correspondent for Hokkaido Shimbun , was arrested on 13 October on Sakhalin Island, in Russia’s Far East, just north of Japan as he was getting ready to leave the country. He was subsequently transferred to Moscow, accused of gathering defence related information for Japanese intelligence – a claim rejected by Japan. Stig Ørskov, WAN-IFRA’s CEO said: “Gathering information in the public interest is a fundamental part of journalism. Security laws must not be used to punish legitimate reporting, intimidate journalists or turn journalists in to bargaining pawns in political disputes.” Imai was working in Russia on a journalist visa, with Russian foreign ministry accreditation. Based in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, his work covered Russia’s Far East and regional relationships. His last report on 5 October, described the presence and everyday lives of North Korean workers on Sakhalin. David Walmsley, President of WAN-IFRA’s World Editors Forum and editor-in-chief of The Globe and Mail said: “The gathering of information by reporters is the entire purpose of responsible journalism and Imai is no different. It is to the dismay of his colleagues across the industry that his responsibility has been perversely turned into accusations of wrongdoing. Imai should be immediately released.” WAN-IFRA urges its members, national media associations and the wider international media community to take every opportunity to protest Russia’s actions, and the intimidation and arrest of journalists.

market.title: Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.
market.summary_raw: Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals. But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor...
market.content_text: Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals . But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution . Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy. “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.” Mongabay, founded in 1999 by Rhett Butler as a one-person news operation covering rainforests, now has 150 people on staff. It produces original content in English, Indonesian, Spanish, French, Hindi, Portuguese, Bengali, and Swahili. Mongabay’s largest bureaus — after the catch-all “global” newsroom — cover Africa (20 people) and Latin America (19 people). Mongabay has about 83,000 followers on Instagram and its English-language YouTube channel has 60,000 subscribers . It also has country-specific channels; Mongabay Indonesia has 109,000 followers. Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries . To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic , The New York Times , ProPublica , and contributing creator Izzy Sasada . An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field . “We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.” Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.) Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. […]

market.title: The New York Times stays on track to reach 15 million subscribers by the end of 2027
market.summary_raw: The New York Times added 420,000 new digital subscribers in the third quarter of 2026, keeping it on track to achieve its goal of hitting 15 million subscriptions by the end of 2027. The Times now has 13.76 million total subscribers, the company said in its earnings report released Wednesday. Almost all of those subscribers...
market.content_text: The New York Times added 420,000 new digital subscribers in the third quarter of 2026, keeping it on track to achieve its goal of hitting 15 million subscriptions by the end of 2027. The Times now has 13.76 million total subscribers, the company said in its earnings report released Wednesday. Almost all of those subscribers — 13.22 million of them — are digital-only. The Times counted 540,000 total print subscribers in the quarter. This time last year, it had 570,000 print subscribers. A few other highlights from the earnings: The Times spent $3.8 million on its ongoing lawsuit against OpenAI during the quarter. In total, it’s spent $36.7 million on generative AI–related lawsuits since it began breaking out those costs separately in earning reports in 2024. In a statement, New York Times Company president and CEO Meredith Kopit Levien referred to “human-made journalism” as one of the Times’ advantages. Affiliate and licensing revenue was up, “primarily as a result of higher licensing and higher Wirecutter affiliate referral revenues.” (Wirecutter is trying to diversify its business model beyond affiliate revenue as AI drives down its organic search traffic.) In the investor call following the earnings report, one investor asked whether the Times expects subscribers to use AI agents to haggle over subscription prices. So far, Kopit Levien said, “we’re not seeing an impact…[but] we’re continually evaluating how third-party automated tools interact with all of our platforms. It’s just worth saying, we have the ability to permit, to restrict, or to block specific tools.” An investor asked about the Times’ video strategy. Kopit Levien’s response in full: Let me just start by saying, we’ve got really big ambitions in video for The Times to be as preferred a brand to watch as it is to read and listen. This is a kind of long bet that we can grow engagement from the audience we have, and also grow audience, because we’re going to engage new people in different ways. I’m not sure what you’re referring to operationally. We’ve been in a sort of steady state of scaling production in the newsroom of video, and that’s happening in myriad ways. We’ve got a big and expansive shows group, and I referred to that in my prepared remarks, where we’re putting a lot of resource and energy into a growing stable of shows that are getting more and more cultural resonance. We also continue to have a big effort on visual investigations, which we’ve referred to in prior quarters and in prepared remarks. I referred today in my prepared remarks to a very big effort in the development of short-form video. We’ve talked about that pretty extensively, so a lot of reporter video. Then also now, we’re rolling out more assertively some short-form video franchises, like the one I mentioned from our fashion critic, Vanessa Friedman. We’ve got another one coming from one of the hosts of The Daily. […]
